Puzzle 1 · 2 of 10

The tree Compose remembers

Every composable call records a group through the Composer, and then returns. Here's where those records go, so that a counter's value survives the call that made it, and the same call finds it again next time.

  • Puzzle 0: What @Composable really does

    The Compose compiler plugin rewrites every @Composable function. It adds a hidden $composer parameter (and a $changed one), and wraps the body in a start and an end, so everything the call records in between forms its group, labelled with a key from its place in the source. Each composable passes its Composer on to the composables it calls, which is why only a composable can call a composable.

The problem

Puzzle 0 showed every composable call recording a group through the Composer, and then returning. When a function returns, its local variables are gone. So where does remember { mutableStateOf(0) } keep that 0 between runs? And when Counter runs again, how does it find its own 0, and not the one from another Counter on the same screen?

See it

The building block

The first time your composables run, the Composer builds the composition: a tree of groups, one per call, nested the way the calls nest. Android's docs put it in one line: "A Composition is a tree-structure of the composables that describe your UI." Unlike the calls, it stays: from then on it's only updated, by recomposition.

Some calls leave more than a group. Text, Button, Column: the composables that end up on screen also leave a node, a real UI element with a size and a place on screen. In Compose's UI library the node class is LayoutNode ("an element in the layout hierarchy"). Your own Greeting and Counter leave only groups: they arrange calls, they aren't elements. So the nodes, taken out of the groups, form a smaller tree of their own: the UI tree, which puzzle 4 turns into pixels.

Groups also keep values, in slots. A slot holds an argument the call got last time (puzzle 3 compares against it) or a value it asked to keep. That's all remember is: in the runtime's own code, remember { … } is a call that asks the current Composer to store the value in the composition, at this group. It doesn't become a global: two Counters are two groups, with two slots and two counts.

The runtime keeps the whole composition in one structure, the slot table: groups and their slots, laid out in the order the calls ran, each group's children right after it. Reading it from start to end is fast; jumping around in it is not, which is why the next run walks it in the same order as the calls.

So how does a call find its slots again? By where it's called from. Each call site, the place in your source where a composable is called, gets its own key from the compiler plugin (puzzle 0). On the next run, the calls come in the same order from the same call sites, so Counter reaches the same group and finds its 0. If an if-statement adds a call above it, Counter still keeps its count: its call site didn't move.

Go deeperWhat does the slot table look like in memory?
Why does the runtime store groups in call order in arrays, instead of as a tree of objects that point at each other?

The next run reads the groups in the same order the calls happen, and a front-to-back scan of an array is fast. The default table is two arrays (one for groups, one for slots) with a gap kept where the next insert goes, so adding a group there doesn't shift everything after it. A linked-list version, faster for moving and deleting content, is being tried behind a flag that's off by default.

Back to the main puzzle

In practice

The one place call sites aren't enough is a loop: every item comes from the same call site, so the runtime tells them apart by their order. Insert an item at the top and every item below gets the slots of the one that used to be in its position. The key() composable fixes it by giving each item an identity of its own: key(movie.id) { MovieRow(movie) }. LazyColumn takes the same idea as a key parameter on its items.

The analogy

The stage manager's prompt book from puzzle 0. The first performance fills it in, scene after scene, with each scene's notes inside it (its group). On some pages there's a set piece that goes on stage (a node). Margins hold what to keep: which hat the hero wore (slots). The next night, the scenes come in the same order, so the stage manager turns to the same page and finds the same hat. A new scene added before it gets a new page; the old pages don't move.

Right. It lives in the slot table, not on the call.

What you now know

The first run of your composables builds the composition, a tree of groups, one per call, nested the way the calls nest, and kept after they return. Composables such as Text and Button also leave a node, a real UI element. Groups keep values in slots (last time's arguments, what you remember), and the runtime stores all of it in call order in the slot table. On the next run, a call finds its own group and slots again by its call site, the place in the code it's called from.
